source_spans.locator: The Journal of Philosophy 101(8) (2004), published pp.389-390, opening scope: target view claims literal environmental components of cognitive states/processes and the paper evaluates that constitutive claim

The Journal of Philosophy 101(8) (2004), published pp.392-396, Section II: heavy organism-environment dependence is separated from treating organism plus environment as one system; epistemological relevance does not entail mereological inclusion; an unclear relevance-based inclusion rule risks proliferating or collapsing system taxonomies

The Journal of Philosophy 101(8) (2004), published pp.421-424, Section VIII: functional-role realizability alone does not independently license external inclusion; the relevant psychofunctional theory must be empirically motivated, and the discussion culminates in the need first to identify what counts as a cognitive system

The Journal of Philosophy 101(8) (2004), published pp.424-427, Section IX: cognitive-system delineation precedes warranted state attribution; the target is a stable integrated cognitive agent, empirical research must motivate the system taxonomy, and functional-role theory alone does not settle the boundary

conditions: proposal that causally or epistemically relevant environmental elements are literal components of the cognitive system being analyzed
temporal_scope: candidate system identity may need to persist across time even when particular environmental elements change

nodes.description: the individual organism treated as the cognitive system while its processing can depend heavily on interaction with environmental elements
environmental element that can be causally important to the organism's cognitive performance without thereby being established as a constitutive component
proposed inclusion rule that treats significant relevance of one thing to understanding another as a reason to study them as one system
candidate grouping that determines whether the organism and selected environmental elements are treated as one cognitive system
organism together with selected environmental elements proposed as a single unified unit of cognitive analysis
requirement for an independently motivated account of a stable integrated cognitive system whose usefulness is supported by empirical and explanatory work rather than mere relevance
attribution of cognitive states or capacities to the selected system as the bearer of the phenomena to be explained
failure mode in which an underconstrained inclusion rule yields many overlapping or short-lived systems or collapses analysis toward very few systems

relations.description: heavy causal or explanatory dependence on an environmental element is distinguished from literal inclusion of that element within the cognitive-system boundary

a relevance-based rule would license grouping organism and environmental element as one system only by supplying a substantive criterion for how much relevance is enough and how overlapping and temporally changing systems are individuated
when the proposed relevance rule is left underconstrained, its application may yield an unacceptable proliferation of overlapping or short-lived systems or an extremely compressed taxonomy
warranted attribution of cognitive states or capacities to a composite candidate system depends on first identifying and motivating the stable integrated system to which the attribution applies
system delineation must earn empirical and explanatory usefulness; functional-role considerations alone do not determine which composite systems should be treated as cognitive systems
